title: Army returns to plan to detonate stored explosives in Iowa Wednesday after appeals court OKs permit | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

The plan to detonate explosive material at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa – a community in the rural southeastern corner of the state – that was delayed for days and seemingly stopped for a few hours is now back on again for Wednesday morning, the US Army said late Monday.

The military is moving forward with the operation after a permit from the Environmental Protection Agency was reinstated by a federal appeals court Monday and following an earlier statement from President Donald Trump saying he also wanted agreement from Iowa’s Democratic governor-elect before allowing it to continue.

Environmental groups filed suit last week to stop the detonation, saying it risks fouling air, contaminating water and harming residents’ health. The Army has argued the stockpile is too unstable to be left alone.

“Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming Governors say the call belongs to the experts,” acting Army Secretary Adam Telle wroteon X. “We are proceeding with the controlled removal in full coordination with all state, local and federal authorities, because the safety of Iowa’s citizens comes first.”

An emergency alert sent to cell phones in the area by the Federal Emergency Management Agency said the detonation will take place Wednesday at 9 a.m. Central Time. It stated some residents within 5 miles southwest of the site may be evacuated and encouraged people within 5 to 20 miles to stay indoors with their windows closed. Telle is scheduled to hold a news conference on the detonation plan in Middletown Tuesday morning.

The planned explosion is meant to deal with nearly five tons of material containing lead azide, a material used to detonate munitions, that is in a particularly unstable state after being stored long-term at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. US Army officials have said they are unable to move the material due to its volatile condition.

The detonation plan, which was announced to the public only five days before its originally scheduled date, was met with criticism by the community, some elected officials and environmental groups as it has the potential to risk lead exposure across the plains of Iowa, and especially near the plant’s home in Middletown.
